narrative:
The model predicted an 81.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class—far below the average of roughly the sixth and fifth deciles among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly suggested difficulty passing the bar.

Your family income bracket was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. Coming from an upper-middle-income background slightly pulled the prediction toward success, consistent with the fact that most accepted students also come from similar or higher income levels. However, this positive influence was not nearly enough to offset the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

Your low LSAT score of 29.5 and undergraduate GPA of 2.3 reinforced the same academic concerns, though they carried less weight than your law-school performance.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record if possible, consider retaking the LSAT, or explore schools and programs with different admissions criteria that place less emphasis on early law-school grades.
